title: Software Restriction / AppLocker Bypass Detection
exclusions: Detects AppLocker audit-only events on endpoints and rule collections whose governed expectation says `enforce`: 8003 for EXE/DLL, 8006 for MSI/script, 8021 for packaged-app execution, and 8024 for packaged-app deployment. Microsoft documents these events as files/apps allowed to run or install but that would have been prevented if AppLocker were enforced. This is evidence of observed audit-mode allowance contradicting local enforcement expectation; it is not proof that malware ran, privilege was gained, or AppLocker was technically bypassed. Enforced block events 8004/8007/8022/8025 show prevention and are operational context, not bypass. The detector does not identify post-launch behavior by an allowed application, Microsoft-documented AppLocker circumvention flags, allow-rule abuse, missing rule collections, policy conversion/application failure 8000, unsupported SKU 8008, packaged-app configuration failure 8027, App Control for Business/Code Integrity events, Software Restriction Policies, application execution on hosts absent from expectation inventory, or actual process/file/network effects. The lookup schema, exact endpoint/collection keys, validity interval, event classes, ten-minute delay, and severity are local controls rather than Microsoft or Splunk defaults. Missing expected hosts/channels/events/fields or lookup drift are source/control-health failures, not enforced policy. This UC makes no automatic policy, process, file, account, host, or network change and no compliance claim.
evidence: After deployment, retain authoritative endpoint/OS/SKU and AppLocker rule-collection inventory; exported effective AppLocker policy and deployment assignment; versioned `applocker_enforcement_expectations` with owners/validity; channel retention and Splunk input/add-on configuration; representative raw 8001/8002–8007/8020–8025 events; independent source, policy-application, collection-mode, and lookup health; version-controlled `windows_applocker_audit_event_on_enforce_expected` saved search, ACL, schedule, dispatch history, and rows; dashboard/alert revisions; approved migration/test exceptions; incident/change disposition; and dated positive, negative, collection, validity-boundary, wrong-provider, duplicate, malformed, delayed, and missing-source tests. Preserve endpoint, source/channel, event ID/class, file/package path/identity, target user/SID/process ID, policy/rule ID, EventRecordID/activity ID, event/index times, expectation/owner/revision, effective policy evidence, and correlated process telemetry under local privacy/security retention. This documentation-only review created no AppLocker, Windows, Splunk, lookup, policy, process, alert, dashboard, or production evidence.

controlTest.positiveScenario: In an isolated lookup, add exact endpoint/collection rows for `endpoint01.example` with `expected_mode=enforce`, integer validity covering a fixed event time, nonblank expectation ID, and policy owner. In matching XML channel fixtures ingest EventCodes 8003, 8006, 8021, and 8024 from provider `Microsoft-Windows-AppLocker`, each with a distinct EventRecordID and representative `UserData_Xml`. Expect four rows mapped respectively to `exe_dll`, `msi_script`, `packaged_app_execution`, and `packaged_app_deployment`, all with signal `audit_allowance_on_enforce_expected`. Equality at `valid_from_epoch` must match; an unauthorized duplicate replay must yield one row.
controlTest.negativeScenario: Expect zero rows for the same audit events when the exact expectation is `audit`, absent, expired, future, malformed, or missing owner/ID; at equality with exclusive `valid_until_epoch`; and for enforced block events 8004/8007/8022/8025, ordinary allow events 8002/8005/8020/8023, 8000/8001/8008/8027, 8028/8029/8039/8040 App Control events, wrong source/provider/type, missing endpoint/record identity, and events outside the closed bucket. Separate source/control-health searches must alert on missing/malformed/conflicting expectation rows, expected enforced collections without trustworthy effective-policy evidence, channel gaps, and policy application failures rather than interpreting zero primary rows as enforcement.

dataSources: Primary sources are XML-rendered AppLocker channels collected from governed Windows endpoints: `XmlWinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-AppLocker/EXE and DLL` for 8003, `.../MSI and Script` for 8006, `.../Packaged app-Execution` for 8021, and `.../Packaged app-Deployment` for 8024, all with `sourcetype=XmlWinEventLog` and provider `Microsoft-Windows-AppLocker`. Required system identity is `dest`, `Computer`, `ComputerName`, or `host`; event identity is EventRecordID/RecordNumber plus source. Preserve EventCode, UserData_Xml and extracted RuleAndFileData fields such as FilePath/FullFilePath, TargetUser, TargetProcessId, PolicyName, RuleId, activity/correlation ID, `_time`, and `_indextime`. The local exact lookup is `applocker_enforcement_expectations(endpoint,rule_collection,expected_mode,valid_from_epoch,valid_until_epoch,expectation_id,policy_owner)`. Supporting sources include 8001 policy applied, allow/block events, exported effective policy, Group Policy/MDM assignment, AppIDSvc state, Security 4688 or Sysmon 1 process creation, Code Integrity/App Control logs, EDR, file/signature/hash/reputation, and change/asset/identity data.
app: Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Windows (`Splunk_TA_windows`, Splunkbase 742) for XML AppLocker channel collection and Windows event extraction. A local security app owns `applocker_enforcement_expectations`, saved search `windows_applocker_audit_event_on_enforce_expected`, source/policy/lookup-health searches, `UserData_Xml` extraction tests, dashboard, exceptions, and routing. Splunk Enterprise Security is optional; Splunk Security Content provides useful AppLocker analytic/extraction examples but is not required.
spl:
index=wineventlog sourcetype="XmlWinEventLog" (source="XmlWinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-AppLocker/EXE and DLL" OR source="XmlWinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-AppLocker/MSI and Script" OR source="XmlWinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-AppLocker/Packaged app-Execution" OR source="XmlWinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-AppLocker/Packaged app-Deployment") EventCode IN (8003,8006,8021,8024) earliest=-15m@m latest=-10m@m
| spath input=UserData_Xml
| eval provider=coalesce(Provider_Name,ProviderName,SourceName), endpoint=lower(coalesce(nullif(trim(dest),""),nullif(trim(Computer),""),nullif(trim(ComputerName),""),nullif(trim(host),""))), event_id=tonumber(EventCode), event_record_id=trim(tostring(coalesce(EventRecordID,RecordNumber))), rule_collection=case(event_id=8003,"exe_dll",event_id=8006,"msi_script",event_id=8021,"packaged_app_execution",event_id=8024,"packaged_app_deployment"), file_path=coalesce('RuleAndFileData.FullFilePath','RuleAndFileData.FilePath',FullFilePath,FilePath), target_user=coalesce('RuleAndFileData.TargetUser',TargetUser,UserName), target_process_id=coalesce('RuleAndFileData.TargetProcessId',TargetProcessId), event_policy_name=coalesce('RuleAndFileData.PolicyName',PolicyName), event_rule_id=coalesce('RuleAndFileData.RuleId',RuleId), activity_id=coalesce(ActivityID,Correlation_ActivityID)
| where provider="Microsoft-Windows-AppLocker" AND len(endpoint)>0 AND endpoint!="-" AND isnotnull(event_id) AND event_id=floor(event_id) AND len(rule_collection)>0 AND len(event_record_id)>0 AND event_record_id!="-"
| eval event_identity=endpoint."|".source."|".event_record_id
| dedup event_identity
| lookup applocker_enforcement_expectations endpoint rule_collection OUTPUT expected_mode valid_from_epoch valid_until_epoch expectation_id policy_owner
| eval valid_from_epoch=tonumber(valid_from_epoch), valid_until_epoch=tonumber(valid_until_epoch), expectation_match=if(expected_mode="enforce" AND isnotnull(valid_from_epoch) AND valid_from_epoch=floor(valid_from_epoch) AND isnotnull(valid_until_epoch) AND valid_until_epoch=floor(valid_until_epoch) AND valid_from_epoch<=_time AND _time<valid_until_epoch AND len(expectation_id)>0 AND len(policy_owner)>0,1,0)
| where expectation_match=1
| eval signal="audit_allowance_on_enforce_expected", local_severity="high", use_case="UC-1.2.102", event_time=strftime(_time,"%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ")
| table _time endpoint source event_id rule_collection signal local_severity file_path target_user target_process_id event_policy_name event_rule_id event_record_id activity_id expected_mode expectation_id policy_owner event_time _indextime use_case
| sort 0 -_time endpoint rule_collection file_path
description: Detects AppLocker audit-only events—software was allowed but would have been blocked—when the endpoint’s exact rule-collection inventory says enforcement should be active. It preserves the affected file/package, target identity, AppLocker policy/rule, source channel, record identity, expectation owner, and timing while avoiding the false claim that a normal enforced block is a bypass.
value: An endpoint believed to enforce application allowlisting can silently permit software when a collection remains in Audit only mode, weakening a control relied upon for malware and unauthorized-software prevention. Correlating Microsoft’s explicit audit-allowance events with governed expectations reduces enforcement-drift detection time and directs remediation to the exact host and collection without treating every blocked or allowed application as malicious.
implementation: Inventory AppLocker-capable endpoints, OS/SKU, deployment mechanism, each EXE/DLL, MSI/script, and packaged-app collection, expected enforcement mode, owner, and validity. Collect all applicable AppLocker channels as XML, validate raw and UserData_Xml fields, and separately prove policy application/effective mode. Save the SPL as `windows_applocker_audit_event_on_enforce_expected`; run every five minutes over a closed bucket delayed ten minutes. Treat 8003/8006/8021/8024 as audit-mode allowances, not technical bypass proof; keep 8004/8007/8022/8025 blocks, 8000/8008/8027 health failures, and 8001 policy application in supporting views. Correlate with effective policy, deployment/change, process creation, file/signature, user, and endpoint evidence before response.
visualization: Dashboard `Windows AppLocker — Enforcement Expectations`: show expected endpoint/collection coverage, OS/SKU eligibility, effective-policy evidence age, latest 8001, AppIDSvc/channel/source health, malformed UserData_Xml, duplicate/late records, and lookup conflicts/expiry first. Show primary audit allowances on enforce-expected collections by endpoint, collection, file/package, target user, policy/rule, and owner; separately trend audit-only, blocked, ordinary allowed, and policy/health events. Drill down to restricted raw XML/UserData_Xml, exported effective AppLocker policy, Group Policy/MDM assignment, service state, process creation/parent, file hash/signature/reputation, user/session, change, and incident evidence. Never render absent AppLocker events or an inventory row alone as proof of enforcement.
schema: Raw XML AppLocker events plus extracted RuleAndFileData and exact enforcement-expectation lookup
dataModelAcceleration: Endpoint.Processes can correlate observed process creation, but it cannot reproduce this primary decision: AppLocker audit event ID, source channel/rule collection, UserData_Xml policy/rule fields, EventRecordID, and time-bounded enforcement expectation. A generic process model also cannot prove effective AppLocker mode. Keep raw AppLocker events authoritative; use a purpose-built summary only after parity tests preserve identity, channel, policy revision, and late/duplicate behavior.

knownFalsePositives:
A result is a genuine AppLocker audit-mode allowance event on a collection locally expected to enforce; it is not necessarily malicious software or a deliberate bypass.

1. **Approved audit-to-enforce migration** — A pilot ring can intentionally remain Audit only while the expectation lookup was advanced too early. Verify endpoint/ring, collection, migration plan, owner, approval, start, exclusive expiry, effective policy, and rollback. Correct expectation timing rather than suppressing indefinitely.

2. **Group Policy or MDM convergence delay** — A newly assigned enforcement policy may not yet be effective because the endpoint was offline, assignment/sync is pending, policy precedence differs, or restart/service requirements remain. Confirm authoritative assignment and actual exported effective policy; intent alone is not enforcement.

3. **Collection-specific mode** — EXE/DLL can enforce while MSI/script or packaged-app collections audit. The detector keys by exact collection. Verify the event’s channel/ID and effective collection mode rather than treating AppLocker as one host-wide switch.

4. **Lab, compatibility, or line-of-business test** — Engineers may deliberately run an application that would be blocked to evaluate rules in an isolated audit ring. Require test endpoint, file/package hash/path, user, test ID, owner, approver, finite window, and cleanup; never test unknown software on production.

5. **Stale or incorrect endpoint identity** — Reimaging, renaming, cloning, duplicate hostnames, or collector host attribution can join an event to the wrong expectation. Correlate device ID/asset record, raw Computer, deployment identity, and collection route before policy changes.

6. **Policy/rule update not reflected in inventory** — A valid emergency or application onboarding change can alter mode or rule content before the expectation workflow updates. Confirm change approval, exported effective policy, event PolicyName/RuleId, and file metadata. Do not backdate records to erase unexplained execution.

7. **Benign software allowed under Audit only** — Updater, installer, script, management, or business software can legitimately generate 8003/8006/8021/8024. The mismatch remains real if enforcement was expected; classify software risk separately from control drift.

8. **Duplicate/replayed event** — WEF plus direct forwarding, restored channel logs, or checkpoint reset can repeat EventRecordID. The SPL deduplicates exact in-window identity; source health must identify and correct persistent replay.

**Safe notification suppression:** use exact endpoint, collection, expectation/test ID, numeric inclusive start, exclusive expiry, owner, approver, ticket, and reason after preserving the base finding. Reject wildcard hosts/collections/files, permanent audit-ring exceptions, and suppression of source, policy-application, service, channel, or expectation-health failures.
mitreAttack: N/A (AppLocker enforcement-mode drift; no attack behavior asserted)
detectionType: Audit-mode allowance on enforce-expected AppLocker collection
reviewer: documentation-only editorial review against current Microsoft AppLocker event, audit/enforce, policy-management, and security-consideration guidance plus Splunk AppLocker analytic and Windows add-on source/configuration documentation; IDs/channels, extraction, lookup, SPL, fixtures, source/control health, dashboard, alerting, and response were specified but not executed or Microsoft/Splunk/AppLocker/endpoint/security-operations SME signed

cost.search_load_notes: The primary search scans four audit event IDs over one closed five-minute bucket, parses UserData_Xml, and performs one exact lookup. AppLocker logs can be verbose—especially EXE and DLL—so supporting allow/block coverage and retention can add substantial ingest.

detailedImplementation:
## Prerequisites and exact signal contract

Assign endpoint engineering, Windows/AppLocker, Group Policy/MDM, application owner, asset/identity, Splunk, SOC, and incident owners. Inventory every governed endpoint: stable device identity and hostname, OS/build/edition, AppLocker support, organizational ring, policy deployment source/precedence, AppIDSvc state, EXE, DLL, MSI, Script, Packaged app-Execution, and Packaged app-Deployment collection presence/mode, policy/rule version, expected enforcement date, owner, and approved exceptions. Keep expected inventory independent from event traffic so a silent endpoint or absent collection cannot appear enforced.

Microsoft distinguishes Audit only from Enforce rules. In Audit only, a file affected by policy is allowed but an event records that it would have been blocked. Current event guidance maps 8003 to EXE/DLL audit allowance, 8006 to script/MSI audit allowance, 8021 to packaged-app execution audit, and 8024 to packaged-app installation/deployment audit. Events 8004, 8007, 8022, and 8025 are enforced blocks; they demonstrate that the named action was prevented under that rule collection and are not bypass evidence.

The primary detector only returns an audit-allowance event when an exact endpoint/collection expectation says Enforce at event time. That is a control-state contradiction. It does not infer why the effective mode differed, whether the file was malicious, whether a process actually persisted, or whether a Microsoft-documented post-launch AppLocker limitation was used. Microsoft warns that AppLocker does not control behavior after allowed applications launch and documents flags such as `SANDBOX_INERT` and `LOAD_IGNORE_CODE_AUTHZ_LEVEL` as potential circumvention paths; these behaviors require process/API/EDR evidence and are not detected by audit-mode events.

Apply least privilege. Forwarders read applicable AppLocker channels; search roles read the index/expectation lookup and schedule. Restrict file paths, user SIDs/names, policy/rule data, package identity, and process correlation. Alert actions require no AppLocker/GPO/MDM, process termination, file quarantine, account, host isolation, or firewall privileges.

## Step 1 — Deploy AppLocker and prove effective policy

Use Microsoft’s AppLocker planning/deployment guidance for the supported Windows editions in scope. Build rules in Audit only, review events and application-owner impact, then move approved collections to Enforce rules through governed Group Policy, MDM/CSP, or local policy. Rule collections can have different modes; record the exact mode per endpoint/ring/collection. Preserve signed/versioned policy XML, assignment, precedence, approvals, rollout/rollback, and exception ownership.

Do not equate assignment with effectiveness. Verify exported effective policy on representative and sampled endpoints after policy refresh, reboot/service requirements, ring transition, and precedence. Track event 8001 (policy applied successfully), event 8000 (conversion failed), 8008 (component unavailable on SKU), 8027 (packaged apps cannot execute while EXE rules enforce and no packaged-app rules exist), AppIDSvc state, Group Policy/MDM status, and collection coverage. A recent 8001 is supporting evidence, not complete proof that every expected collection and rule is effective.

Microsoft lists AppLocker event channels under **Applications and Services Logs > Microsoft > Windows > AppLocker**: EXE and DLL; MSI and Script; Packaged app-Execution; and Packaged app-Deployment. Collect all channels applicable to the collections you claim. Package/application behavior and newer App Control events can differ by Windows release; qualify exact IDs against the deployed OS and current Microsoft documentation.

## Step 2 — Collect XML and govern the expectation lookup

With a supported Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Windows, enable each channel in an app-owned `local/inputs.conf` stanza with XML rendering and the governed index. Do not edit the add-on’s `default` directory. Validate resulting sources exactly; representative names are the four `XmlWinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-AppLocker/...` values in sidecar `spl`, with `sourcetype=XmlWinEventLog`.

Compare the same EventRecordID in Event Viewer and Splunk. Verify provider, source/channel, EventCode, Computer/dest, EventRecordID, ActivityID where present, UserData_Xml, RuleAndFileData.FilePath/FullFilePath, TargetUser, TargetProcessId, PolicyName, RuleId, `_time`, and `_indextime`. Splunk Security Content demonstrates `spath input=UserData_Xml` and `RuleAndFileData.*` for AppLocker analytics; actual nested fields vary by event/version, so retain coalesces and test every selected ID. Field absence belongs in extraction health, not an invented value.

Create `applocker_enforcement_expectations.csv` with exact lowercase `endpoint,rule_collection,expected_mode,valid_from_epoch,valid_until_epoch,expectation_id,policy_owner`. Allowed collection keys are `exe_dll`, `msi_script`, `packaged_app_execution`, and `packaged_app_deployment`; allowed modes are `audit` and `enforce`. Require integer inclusive-start/exclusive-expiry boundaries, immutable expectation ID, owner, approver/change in controlled metadata, and no wildcards. Publish atomically through maker/checker review.

Create expectation health for duplicates/conflicts, malformed times, start >= expiry, blank owner/ID, unknown endpoint/collection, unsupported OS/SKU, absent collection, expired/near-expiry rows, policy revision mismatch, and inventory drift. Missing/malformed expectation is not a primary match because effective intent is unknown; the health control must page the policy owner rather than silently calling it audit or enforce.

Create channel/source health that compares expected endpoints/collections to recent events or independent configuration telemetry. Report missing endpoint/channel, stale 8001/config evidence, 8000/8008/8027, AppIDSvc fault, provider/source/type drift, malformed UserData_Xml, blank event identity, duplicate route, future event, indexing delay, forwarder backlog, log overwrite/clear, and volume collapse/spike. Quiet audit/block events can be normal; do not use a violation as the only heartbeat.

## Step 3 — Create and understand the primary SPL

Save sidecar `spl` verbatim as `windows_applocker_audit_event_on_enforce_expected`. Schedule every five minutes with a ten-minute delay. At 12:15, `earliest=-15m@m latest=-10m@m` covers 12:00 through but not including 12:05. Measure p99 event delay; move both bounds together while preserving nonoverlap and add reviewed reconciliation for late records.

The base search fixes XML, four exact channels, four audit-only event IDs, and one closed bucket. `spath` extracts nested UserData_Xml. `eval` normalizes endpoint and event identity, maps each event ID to one rule collection, and coalesces file, user, process, policy, and rule fields from nested or top-level extraction. `where` requires the Microsoft AppLocker provider and trusted identity. Endpoint/source/EventRecordID deduplicates exact replay.

The exact lookup then supplies expected mode, validity, expectation ID, and owner. A row survives only when mode is literally `enforce`, both boundaries are integer, `_time` is in `[valid_from,valid_until)`, and ID/owner are nonblank. One event produces one finding; no count, file-name, location, user, or reputation threshold is claimed. `high` is local control severity, not a Microsoft event level.

No Endpoint.Processes `tstats` search can substitute. Process telemetry answers whether a process started and what parent/image/user it had; the primary answer requires an AppLocker audit disposition, exact channel/collection, policy/rule, record, and enforcement expectation. Correlate rather than conflate.

## Step 4 — Validate events, policy edges, and effects

Use fixed-time synthetic XML/UserData fixtures from `controlTest`. Assert endpoint, source, event ID/collection, file/user/process/policy/rule, EventRecordID, expected mode, expectation ID/owner, signal, severity, event/index time, and UC ID. Test all four IDs/channels; nested/top-level fields; active/audit/absent/expired/future/malformed expectation; equality at inclusive start/exclusive end; duplicate/conflicting lookup; missing owner/ID; wrong provider/channel/type; 8004/8007/8022/8025 blocks; ordinary allow; 8000/8001/8008/8027; 8028/8029/8039/8040; null identity; replay; bucket edges; late/future data; and rerun.

In an isolated AppLocker lab with disposable files/packages and test users, deploy each collection in Audit only and run an item intentionally not allowed by policy. Confirm the documented audit event and that process/package behavior matches the event semantics. Move through the approved Enforce transition and verify the corresponding block event. Compare Event Viewer, exported effective policy, deployment state, Splunk, and Security/Sysmon/EDR process evidence. Do not execute malware, weaken production policy, or use a production privileged endpoint for validation.

Test policy precedence, offline endpoint convergence, reimage/rename, unsupported SKU, AppIDSvc fault, malformed policy, missing collection, and rollback. Validate that one collection can audit while another enforces. Test source health independently by stopping a lab forwarder or using fixture gaps, not by hiding production logs.

Measure channel events/second, log retention, ingest bytes, index delay, parse completeness, duplicate rate, search runtime/skips, expectation lookup health, finding rate, alert delivery, effective-policy evidence age, and process-correlation coverage. Keep `status=draft` until endpoint, AppLocker, deployment, application, Splunk, privacy, and SOC owners accept IDs, channels, expectations, fixtures, health, dashboard, routing, exceptions, and response.

## Step 5 — Triage and respond without overclaiming

Alert title should say `AppLocker audit allowance observed where enforcement is expected`; never `AppLocker bypass succeeded` without independent proof. Include endpoint/collection, file/package, target user/process, policy/rule, source/event/record, expectation/owner, event/index delay, effective-policy evidence age, deployment ring/change, source/control health, and restricted raw link.

Responder sequence:
1. Verify raw event, provider/source/ID, EventRecordID, nested extraction, event/index time, replay, and exact expectation revision.
2. Confirm Microsoft event semantics for the deployed Windows release and whether the item was allowed under Audit only. Check channel/collection and file/package identity.
3. Export/inspect effective AppLocker policy and mode on the endpoint; compare Group Policy/MDM assignment, precedence, sync, ring, 8001/8000/8008/8027, AppIDSvc, OS/SKU, reboot/state, and approved change.
4. Correlate process creation/parent, command line, user/session, file hash/signature/publisher/source/prevalence/reputation, network/file effects, EDR alerts, and application owner. An audit event alone does not prove malicious effect.
5. Determine whether this is planned migration, convergence delay, stale expectation, policy/configuration defect, benign software gap, or suspicious execution. Escalate control drift and security behavior through their respective owners.
6. For suspected true bypass through an allowed app or App Control interaction, collect appropriate process/API/Code Integrity/EDR evidence; this detector does not establish that mechanism.

Never automatically terminate a process, quarantine/delete a file, disable an account, isolate a host, change AppLocker/GPO/MDM policy, force policy refresh/reboot, or block network access from this result. Policy changes can break line-of-business applications and audit events can be expected during migration. Authorized responders act only after effective-state and impact validation with rollback.

Closure requires documented cause; corrected expectation or effective collection mode; healthy source/policy/service evidence; application/security disposition; approved policy revision where needed; and no unexplained recurrence across a reviewed interval. Adding an `audit` expectation solely to silence the detector is not remediation. Retain artifacts under local policy; 90 days is advisory.

## Step 6 — Troubleshoot unknowns

- **No AppLocker events:** verify OS/SKU, policy/collection presence, channel enabled/retention, AppIDSvc, local Event Viewer, input/forwarder/index/RBAC, exact source, event time, and expectation/source health.
- **8003/8006/8021/8024 on expected enforce:** check effective per-collection mode, policy precedence/merge, deployment sync, stale inventory, ring/change, and endpoint identity before calling bypass.
- **UserData fields null:** inspect raw UserData_Xml and event version, add-on placement, `spath`, field quoting, truncation, and WEF rendering. Preserve raw evidence; do not guess PolicyName or path.
- **Block events absent:** verify the test item truly falls outside allow rules and the collection is enforced. Ordinary allow rules, missing collection, policy failure, and unsupported SKU are distinct.
- **Endpoint renamed/reimaged:** join through authoritative device identity in a separately reviewed enrichment; hostname-only expectations can become stale.
- **Duplicate rows:** compare endpoint/source/EventRecordID and `_indextime`, WEF/direct routes, restored logs, checkpoint reset, and schedules. Keep distinct event records even for one launch.
- **Process telemetry disagrees:** align event/process time, process ID reuse, script-host behavior, package operations, audit semantics, sensor health, and child processes. AppLocker audit means allowed; it does not promise every sensor reports the same abstraction.
- **CIM count differs:** compare source scope, tags, process-only coverage, acceleration lag, policy mode, and time bounds. Raw AppLocker events plus effective expectation remain authoritative.
grandmaExplanation: We check whether Windows says it allowed a program only because the app rules were in test mode, even though that computer was supposed to be blocking. That helps the team fix a weak setting without pretending every blocked program or test run was an attack.
hardware: AppLocker-capable Windows endpoints and servers with governed EXE/DLL, MSI/script, or packaged-app collections. Validate supported Windows edition/SKU and policy behavior for the deployed release. Software Restriction Policies, App Control for Business/WDAC, managed installer/ISG, non-Windows allowlisting, and EDR application control require separate contracts.
